title: Making crochet buttons
subtitle: Covering a button mould or working a flat disc to use as a button on a crochet garment
excerpt: Crochet buttons are either a small flat disc worked in the round and stuffed slightly to give them depth, or a bought button mould covered with a crocheted fabric panel. Either type can be matched exactly to the garment yarn and eliminates the problem of finding a button that goes with the project.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework, 1886, Project Gutenberg #20776. Weldon's Practical Crochet, 1880s to 1900s, Internet Archive. Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins).

glossaryTerms.definition: A two-part plastic or metal blank with a shank on the back, sold for covering with fabric or crochet. The front plate clips onto the back plate and holds the covering in place.
A small flat disc worked in the round in tight double crochet (UK), sometimes padded with a layer of wadding or a coin-sized offcut of felt, used as a handmade button.

content.text: A crochet button is either a small disc worked in the round and padded, or a
button mould

covered with a crocheted panel. Both produce a button that matches the garment yarn exactly. The disc method needs no extra supplies; the mould method uses a bought two-part blank that holds the crochet cover securely.
What you need

items.name: Fine yarn or thread to match the garment
items.note: A 4-ply or fingering weight gives a neater finish on small buttons than DK or aran.

items.name: Crochet hook, 1.5 mm to 2.5 mm
items.note: Sized to the thread. The fabric should be tight enough that stuffing does not show through.

items.name: Button mould (optional)
items.note: For covered-button method. Size 18 (11 mm) and size 22 (14 mm) are the most useful sizes for garments.

items.name: Small amount of fibrefill or felt disc
items.note: For the disc method , giving the button its slight dome

items.name: Tapestry needle
items.note: For closing the button and sewing it to the garment

content.text: Method 1: the crochet disc
A
crochet button disc
for a 15 mm button:
Magic ring. Round 1: 6 dc (UK) into the ring. Pull tight. (6 sts)
Round 2: 2 dc (UK) in every stitch. (12 sts)
Round 3: [1 dc (UK), 2 dc (UK) in next st] 6 times. (18 sts)
The disc should now measure roughly 3 cm across. If you need a larger button, work one more increase round.

Place a small piece of fibrefill or a circle of thick felt behind the disc. Thread the tail through each remaining stitch and pull firmly to close the button around the padding, forming a slight dome.
Pass the needle several times through the centre of the button from front to back to form the thread shank. This shank is what you sew through to attach the button to the garment.
Method 2: covering a button mould
Work a disc as above, but do not pad it. The disc should be 20 to 25% wider than the button mould face.
Place the crochet disc over the front of the button mould, centering the disc.
Fold the edges of the disc over the back plate and clip the back plate into place. The mould mechanism grips the fabric edges and holds the disc taut over the front.
Common problems

items.symptom: The padding shows through the face of the button
items.cause: The hook size is too large, leaving gaps in the fabric, or the thread is too thin for the crochet tension.
items.fix: Work at a tighter tension or go down one hook size. Check that the fabric is dense enough to hide the stuffing before closing the button.

items.symptom: The button disc is too floppy and does not hold its dome shape
items.cause: Not enough stuffing was used, or the gather was not pulled tight enough.
items.fix: Undo the closing gather, add more fibrefill, and re-close. Pull the gather firmly enough that the button holds its shape without being compressed.

items.symptom: The covered mould is loose and the disc slides under the cover
items.cause: The disc is too small for the mould, so it is not gripped firmly when the back clips on.
items.fix: Make a larger disc: add one increase round and try again. The disc should extend 5 to 7 mm beyond the edge of the mould face when laid flat on top of it.

content.text: What to try next

Work six matching buttons for a cardigan: one in each round of increasing from the pattern above to find the size that best matches the buttonholes. Store spare buttons in the same colourway on a card with a tail of yarn, so replacement buttons for future use can be worked in the matching dye lot.
